topic: The "how much roughly?" question is a test of confidence, and dodging it loses the job.

slides.subtitle: (and most of us fail it)
slides.scene: A gloved hand resting on a steering wheel with a phone held loosely against it, the screen showing a plain pale blue rectangle, seen from the driver seat of a work van in flat daylight. All vehicles, buildings, doors and surfaces in shot have COMPLETELY BLANK panels with absolutely no writing, no company name, no logo, no lettering, no phone number and no graphics of any kind. No signage anywhere in the scene. There is NO text, no words, no numbers and no labels anywhere in the image.

caption:
Did you know that when somebody asks how much it roughly costs, they are not really asking for a number?

They are finding out whether you are straight with them.

The instinct is to dodge it. Every job is different, I would have to see it, I cannot say without looking. All true. And what the customer hears is that you will not tell them, which is what they were worried about.

The contractor who says most of these run between this and this, depending on what we find, does not lose money on that sentence. They win the visit. And they filter out the person who was never going to spend that anyway, which saves a drive.

Dodging feels safe. It reads as evasive.

This one question probably decides more first calls than anything else on the phone.

Comment QUOTE and I will send the breakdown.
